possible_causes: Microphone cable not connected or faulty
Phantom power (+48V) not enabled for condenser microphone
Mute button engaged on mixer channel
Gain/trim set to zero on mixer channel
Faulty XLR connector
troubleshooting_steps: Check that the XLR cable is firmly connected at both the microphone and mixer ends
If using a condenser microphone, verify that phantom power (+48V) is enabled on the mixer channel
Check that the mute button on the mixer channel is not engaged
Turn up the gain/trim control on the mixer channel to an appropriate level
Test with a known-working cable to rule out a cable fault
Test the microphone on a different channel to rule out a channel fault
Test a different microphone on the same channel to confirm whether the fault is in the microphone or the channel
reasoning: No audio from a microphone is most commonly caused by signal chain interruption — a disconnected cable, absent phantom power, or a muted/zero-gain channel — rather than internal hardware failure. These are all quick checks that can be performed without tools.

possible_causes: Gain/trim on the mixer channel set too low
Master fader or channel fader set too low
Amplifier output level set too low
Microphone placed too far from the sound source
Incorrect microphone type for the application (e.g. dynamic mic in a quiet studio environment)
Speaker cable impedance mismatch reducing output
troubleshooting_steps: Check and increase the gain/trim on the mixer channel
Check that the channel fader and master fader are set to an appropriate level
Check the amplifier output level and increase if necessary
Move the microphone closer to the sound source
Check that the speaker cables are securely connected
Test with a different microphone to compare output levels
Check for any active attenuation pads that may be reducing the signal
reasoning: Low volume is almost always a gain-staging issue somewhere in the signal chain — gain, fader, or amplifier levels that are set too conservatively. Physical placement and cable integrity should also be verified before suspecting hardware failure.

possible_causes: Gain/trim set too high on the mixer channel, causing clipping
Input signal level exceeding the mixer's headroom
Amplifier being driven beyond its rated output power
Damaged speaker cone or voice coil
Faulty microphone capsule producing a distorted signal
Incorrect phantom power applied to a dynamic microphone
troubleshooting_steps: Reduce the gain/trim on the mixer channel to eliminate clipping (peak LED should not stay lit)
Check the mixer's input level meters — the signal should peak in the green/amber range, not red
Reduce the amplifier volume if the amplifier is being overdriven
Test the speaker with a known-good audio source to check for a damaged cone
Test with a different microphone to determine if the distortion is originating from the microphone
Verify that phantom power is only enabled on channels connected to condenser microphones
If distortion persists after all adjustments, the microphone or speaker may require professional inspection
reasoning: Distortion is typically caused by clipping — a signal that exceeds the headroom of a device in the chain. The most common culprit is excessive gain at the mixer input. If distortion persists after gain reduction, hardware damage (speaker cone, microphone capsule) is likely and professional inspection is recommended.

possible_causes: Ground loop caused by multiple devices on different electrical circuits
Unbalanced cables picking up electromagnetic interference
Fluorescent lighting or dimmer switches near the cables
Damaged or improperly shielded cable
Nearby power cables running parallel to audio cables
Faulty earth/ground connection on audio equipment
troubleshooting_steps: Power all audio equipment from the same electrical circuit or power strip to eliminate ground loops
Replace unbalanced (TS/RCA) cables with balanced (XLR/TRS) cables where possible
Move audio cables away from mains power cables, dimmer switches, and fluorescent lights
Test with a different cable to rule out a damaged cable
Use a direct injection (DI) box to convert unbalanced signals to balanced signals
Check that all equipment chassis are properly earthed/grounded
If using a laptop on stage, try disconnecting the laptop charger to see if it eliminates the hum
reasoning: A persistent hum or buzz is the classic symptom of a ground loop or electromagnetic interference (EMI). Ground loops occur when equipment connected together shares multiple ground paths at different potentials. The fix is almost always routing — same power circuit, balanced cables, and physical separation from power sources.

possible_causes: Microphone too close to or pointing directly at a speaker
Gain/monitor level set too high
Microphone gain set above the feedback threshold for the room
Incorrect microphone polar pattern selected for the environment
No high-pass filter applied, allowing low-frequency feedback buildup
Excessive reverb or delay causing signal reinforcement
troubleshooting_steps: Immediately reduce the microphone gain or channel fader to stop the feedback
Reposition the microphone so it does not point toward any speaker
Reduce the overall monitor or PA level
Apply a high-pass filter (HPF) at 80–100 Hz to remove low-frequency feedback
Use a graphic equaliser to identify and cut the feedback frequency
Move the microphone closer to the sound source so that gain can be reduced while maintaining level
Select a microphone with a cardioid or supercardioid polar pattern to improve rear rejection
If using in-ear monitors, consider switching from floor monitors to reduce feedback risk
reasoning: Acoustic feedback (the loud squeal) occurs when the microphone picks up its own amplified signal from the speakers and re-amplifies it in a loop. The immediate fix is always to reduce gain. The long-term fix is gain-before-feedback optimisation: correct microphone placement, polar pattern selection, and equalization of problem frequencies.

possible_causes: Faulty or disconnected cable on the affected channel
Mixer channel fader or send level set to zero
Pan control fully set to the opposite side
Channel muted or assigned to an incorrect bus
Faulty channel strip on the mixer
Amplifier channel input or output connector damaged
Damaged speaker driver on one side
troubleshooting_steps: Check that the cable on the affected channel is firmly connected at both ends
Test with a known-working cable on the affected channel
Check the pan control on the mixer channel — it should be centred for both channels
Verify the channel fader is raised and the channel is not muted
Check the channel's bus assignment to ensure it is routed to the correct output
Test the affected channel with a different source to determine if the fault is in the channel or the source
Swap left and right speaker cables to determine whether the fault is in the mixer/amplifier or the speaker
If the mixer channel is confirmed faulty, use an alternative channel
reasoning: A single dead channel narrows the fault to either the cable feeding that channel, the channel strip itself, or the output path from the mixer to the speaker. Systematic substitution (swap cables, swap channels, swap speakers) quickly isolates which component is at fault. A dead mixer channel strip typically requires service.

possible_causes: Faulty or damaged audio cable with an intermittent connection
Dirty or oxidised connector
Loose connector or worn cable at the plug
Faulty channel fader or potentiometer with dirty contacts
Loose internal soldering in a connector or device
Wireless microphone with low battery or signal dropout
troubleshooting_steps: Flex and wiggle the cable while listening — if the crackling changes, the cable is the fault
Replace the cable with a known-working cable to confirm
Clean connector contacts with contact cleaner spray
Check the fader and channel controls on the mixer — crackling while moving a control indicates dirty contacts
If using a wireless microphone, replace the batteries and check the receiver signal strength
Test each cable individually by substitution to isolate the faulty one
Inspect connectors for bent pins, loose sleeves, or visible damage
If a fader is confirmed as the cause, cleaning with contact cleaner or fader replacement may be required
reasoning: Crackling or intermittent audio is almost always a physical connection problem — a damaged cable, dirty connector, or worn potentiometer. The diagnostic method is systematic substitution: replace cables one at a time while listening for the crackling to disappear, then flex cables to confirm intermittency.

fault_name: No Audio Output – Speaker / Amplifier / Mixer
possible_causes: Speaker or amplifier not powered on, or power cable disconnected
Speaker cable disconnected or faulty
Amplifier output level set to zero or muted
Mixer master fader at zero or main output muted
Incorrect output routing on the mixer (signal sent to wrong bus)
Blown speaker driver or damaged amplifier output stage
Faulty power amplifier channel
troubleshooting_steps: Check that the speaker or amplifier is powered on and the power cable is connected
Verify the speaker cable is firmly connected at both the amplifier output and speaker input
Test with a known-working speaker cable to rule out a cable fault
Check the amplifier output level or gain control is not set to zero
Check the mixer master fader is raised and the main output is not muted
Verify the mixer output routing – confirm the channel is assigned to the main L/R bus
Test the speaker with a different amplifier or audio source to isolate the fault
Test the amplifier with a different speaker to determine whether the fault is in the amplifier or the speaker
If no output is detected from the amplifier at all, professional inspection may be required
reasoning: No audio from a speaker or amplifier is most commonly caused by a power, cable, or routing issue in the signal chain. Systematic substitution – swapping cables, testing with alternate sources, and checking mixer routing – will isolate whether the fault is in the speaker, the amplifier, or the mixer output stage.
